lesson.title: A language model, and changing one
lesson.subtitle: Only the top block

video.title: A language model, and changing one: Only the top block
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours. Narration in the lesson language. Captions are separate files.
cast: Joseph - computer studies teacher, talking to a fellow lecturer
Narrator - the Darsi voice, warm and precise, talking to a university lecturer

scenes.narration: A paragraph that says we fine-tuned the model, with no layer named, is incomplete. The frozen part has to be visible.
In the seminar: next token, a frozen stack, and a rubric line that unnamed weights score zero.
The small fine-tune teaches only the top block, on a few examples. The rest of the weights do not move.
That is the honest version a phone can run. It will not absorb a library.
An old skill can be crowded out. Say which part moved before you say the model learned.
Here the lower blocks stay still. Only the top block is allowed to change.
Quick check! Fine-tuning, in the small lab, changes which of these?
The top block, on a few examples. The rest stays frozen.
Mark only write-ups that name the frozen layers. Warn that a confident rewrite of an old fact is the crowding, not a feature.
Your turn. Does a language model look facts up as it writes?
Remember this. Name the layer that moved. An old skill can slip.
Try it in your next lecture. Three answers that say the model was fine-tuned, and the same reason each scores zero.

checkpoints.prompt: Fine-tuning, in the small lab, changes which of these?

options.text: Every weight, starting again from random numbers
Only the list of words the model knows
The top block, on a few examples

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the rest stays frozen. That is the honest small version.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the small lab changes the top block, on a few examples.

checkpoints.prompt: Does a language model look facts up as it writes?

options.text: No, it guesses the next token
Yes, it rereads its training data

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: it guesses the next token from patterns, unless a separate tool searches.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a language model guesses the next token. It does not look facts up.
